blocks.text: INNNEWS - Sukidi's post in the day compass called Espaz Alarm (November 13, 2025) echoed like a midnight bell in public space that was beginning to lose its hearing. He writes with the quiet of a scientist, but also with professional anxiety. Among the growing political fog, his words were the axis of awareness that this nation was returning to dangerous crossroads: between freedom and fear, between law and power, between conscience and interest.

What's surprising is that not only is the content of the analysis that many of us actually know the direction of this wind, but the moral clarity that radiates from its writing. Amidst the silent culture, Sukidi chose to speak. In the midst of social apathy, it reminds him that authoritarianism does not come with the sound of tanks, but with a face of legality and the language of morality. He cited Levitsky and Ziblatt about the Espautized State, revealing that law enforcement could be a political weapon. Here, Sukidi is writing not only political opinion, but professional text in secular form.
But at that point, a bitter question arose: why is the professional voice now coming from outside of the church?

For centuries, the church was known as the moral beacon of the world... to a place where the conscience of nations is purified and the direction history is checked. But now, too many spiritual leaders are more busy with symbols than substance. The Church is trapped in its comfort, forgetting that its true gospel is news disturbing the calm of powerful men.

We talk about love, but avoid the risk of justice. We preach peace, but fear reprimand. In public space, the church seems to lose relevance not because of lack of faith, but because of loss of courage. While Sukidi is a Muslim who writes with national sense it shows what it means to have faith in humanity and justice.
In this context, Sukidi's writing is a mirror for the church: when theologians are busy arguing about safety terminology, an Islamic scholar is fighting for the safety of the nation.

Democracy, like faith, relieves on trust. He's fragile without honesty, and empty without morality. When Sukidi said to us, "Be patient in human being," it is not just a call that should be familiar in the ears of the faithful.

Jesus once said, "The truth will set you free." In fact, democracy can't live without the spirit of courage to declare the truth even if it's unpopular. And precisely here, the church should stand at the front of it as a guardian of the nation's freedom of conscience.

However, as Sukidi warned, the political fear of being a system has turned into fear. Connotation and intimidation are now operating subtly behind the jargon of morality. At the same time, many religious leaders are more concerned about losing influence than losing the truth.

The biggest challenge of the church is not from outside, but quiet from within. We have thousands of pulses, but a little bit of professional noise. We have systematic theology, but poor social empathy. We established a spiritual institution of education, but failed to give birth to a public thinker that shook the nation's conscience.

Sukidi's writing realized that true intelligence was born of moral courage. It shows that being intellectual means not neutral in the face of injustice. In Bible language, he has done what many churches have forgotten: voiced unconditional religious truth.

The Church should learn this kind of clarity, not feel threatened by it. For if we truly believe that the Spirit works throughout all human history, then conscience is right for no stranger but the reflection of the Truth itself. "

When the law is held selectively and chop-chop, democracy falls, Sukidi writing. The sentence echoed not only for the country, but also for the church. Because even churches can fall into spiritual authoritarianism when truth is monopolized, and courage is sacrificed in the name of stability.

Now, the question we have to answer is not whether the alarm is ringing, it's whether we can still hear it. For if this nation's moral ear continues to be shut, then as Sukidi wrote, so the ghost of authoritarianism roams with political fear.

Perhaps, it is time for the church to repent of love not of sin of the world, but of sin of silence. Because in the history of salvation, God often used the sound of outside the walls of faith to reprimand his people who slept. Today, that voice came from a Sukidi. And perhaps, God is talking through him to all of us:
Wake up, church. The world is waiting for your voice.
